title: As Federal Court Rules ALPRs are Mass Surveillance, EFF Gets Disappointing Ruling
summary: A California trial court dismissed SIREN v. San Jose, EFF and ACLU-NC's challenge to San Jose police's warrantless searches of its ALPR database, finding no reasonable expectation of privacy on public roads. EFF plans to appeal and contrasts the ruling with a federal district court decision in Oklahoma issued a day earlier that called ALPRs 'indiscriminate mass surveillance' and held a warrantless Flock search violated the Fourth Amendment.

key_quotes.quote: a California trial court dismissed SIREN v. San Jose, our case challenging the city of San Jose's warrantless searches of its vast stores of automated license plate reader (ALPR) data

a federal district court in Oklahoma called ALPRs "a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance" and decided that a law enforcement officer's warrantless search of ALPR data violated the Fourth Amendment
It blankets the city's streets in nearly five hundred cameras that continuously photograph every car that passes by and retains the collected data for a month or longer
